# Exercise 4.4 — The decision boundary {#sec-decision-boundary}

In Exercise 4.1 the map of the logistic regression's probability had a black
line across it: to one side the model says `pos`, to the other `neg`. That line
is the **decision boundary**. In this exercise you work it out from the
coefficients, see why it is straight, move it with the threshold, and meet data
where no straight line can do the job.

- **Part 1.** Find the boundary of the glucose and BMI model by hand, and check
  it on the map.
- **Part 2.** Change the threshold, as in Exercise 4.3, and see the line move.
- **Part 3.** A dataset where the risk is high at both ends of a measurement.
  A straight boundary fails; a squared term or a tree gives a boundary that
  bends.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## The plots are for looking at
The code for the plots is folded away under **Code for this plot
(optional)**. You do not need to write it, but it is in the download if you
want it.
:::

### Packages and data

```{r}
# Packages for this exercise. If one is missing, remove the # and run this line once:
# install.packages(c("tidyverse", "tidymodels"))

library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)

theme_set(theme_bw())
```

The same 750 people and the same split as in Exercise 4.1.

```{r}
diabetes <- read_csv("data/diabetes_clean.csv") |>
  select(glucose, mass, diabetes) |>
  mutate(diabetes = factor(diabetes, levels = c("neg", "pos")))

test_rows <- seq(1, nrow(diabetes), by = 5)     # every fifth person is held back
train <- diabetes[-test_rows, ]
test  <- diabetes[test_rows, ]
```

### Part 1 — Where the class changes

Fit the model from Exercise 4.1, Part 2: diabetes from glucose and BMI.

```{r}
log_model <- logistic_reg() |>
  set_engine("glm") |>
  set_mode("classification")

log_fit <- log_model |>
  fit(diabetes ~ glucose + mass, data = train)

b <- log_fit$fit$coefficients      # intercept, glucose, BMI
b
```

The model is a straight line on the log-odds scale (Exercise 4.2):

$$\text{log-odds} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{glucose} + \beta_2 \times \text{BMI}$$

With a threshold of 0.5, the class changes where the probability is 0.5. A
probability of 0.5 is odds of 1 and **log-odds of 0**. So the boundary is every
combination of glucose and BMI where

$$\beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{glucose} + \beta_2 \times \text{BMI} = 0$$

For a given BMI, solve for glucose:

$$\text{glucose} = \frac{-\beta_0 - \beta_2 \times \text{BMI}}{\beta_1}$$

#### Task 1a — The boundary at a BMI of 30 and of 45

Round the coefficients printed above to four significant figures and calculate,
by hand, the glucose at which the class changes for a BMI of 30. Then do the
same for a BMI of 45.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
boundary_30 <- (-(______) - ______ * 30) / ______
boundary_45 <- (-(______) - ______ * 45) / ______
c(boundary_30, boundary_45)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
In order: the intercept, the BMI weight, and the glucose weight. The intercept
is negative, so minus the intercept is a positive number.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
boundary_30 <- (-(-7.004) - 0.06437 * 30) / 0.03355
boundary_45 <- (-(-7.004) - 0.06437 * 45) / 0.03355
c(boundary_30, boundary_45)
```

At a BMI of 30 the class changes at a glucose of about 151 mg/dL; at a BMI of
45, at about 122.
:::
:::

Check it with `predict()`: a patient on the boundary should get a probability
of 0.5.

```{r}
predict(log_fit, new_data = data.frame(glucose = 151.2, mass = 30), type = "prob")
```

Every point on the boundary satisfies one linear equation in glucose and BMI,
so the boundary is a **straight line**. Here it is, drawn from the
coefficients, over the test patients:

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
# the boundary written as BMI = a + s * glucose
ggplot(test, aes(x = glucose, y = mass, shape = diabetes, colour = diabetes)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_abline(intercept = -b[1] / b[3], slope = -b[2] / b[3], linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("point", x = c(151.2, 122.4), y = c(30, 45), colour = "red", size = 3) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(neg = 1, pos = 17)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(neg = "steelblue", pos = "darkorange")) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(40, 200), ylim = c(18, 68)) +
  labs(x = "Glucose (mg/dL)", y = "BMI (kg/m²)", shape = "Measured", colour = "Measured",
       title = "The decision boundary at a threshold of 0.5")
```

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Think about it
1. The model is right for 76% of the test patients. Looking at the plot, why
   can no straight line do much better with these two measurements?
2. A model with three predictors (glucose, BMI and age) also has a boundary.
   What shape would it be?
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
1. Patients with and without diabetes overlap heavily: there are triangles
   well to the left of the line and circles well to the right. Glucose and BMI
   do not hold enough information to separate them, whatever line you draw.
2. Still flat: one linear equation in three measurements is a flat plane in
   three dimensions. A logistic regression always has a flat boundary in the
   predictors you give it.
:::
:::

### Part 2 — The threshold moves the line

Exercise 4.3 changed the threshold. A threshold $t$ is a probability, so it has
a log-odds, $\log\big(t / (1 - t)\big)$, and the boundary is where the model's
log-odds equal it:

$$\beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{glucose} + \beta_2 \times \text{BMI} = \log\left(\frac{t}{1-t}\right)$$

Only the right-hand side changes, so the line keeps its tilt and moves
sideways.

#### Task 2a — The log-odds of three thresholds

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
thresholds <- data.frame(t = c(0.3, 0.5, 0.7)) |>
  mutate(log_odds = log(______ / (1 - ______)),
         glucose_at_BMI_30 = (log_odds - b[1] - b[3] * 30) / b[2])

thresholds
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
Both blanks are the threshold column, `t`.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
thresholds <- data.frame(t = c(0.3, 0.5, 0.7)) |>
  mutate(log_odds = log(t / (1 - t)),
         glucose_at_BMI_30 = (log_odds - b[1] - b[3] * 30) / b[2])

thresholds
```

The log-odds are −0.847, 0 and 0.847. At a BMI of 30 the class changes at a
glucose of 126, 151 and 176 mg/dL.
:::
:::

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
lines_t <- data.frame(t = factor(c(0.3, 0.5, 0.7)),
                      log_odds = log(c(0.3, 0.5, 0.7) / (1 - c(0.3, 0.5, 0.7)))) |>
  mutate(intercept = (log_odds - b[1]) / b[3], slope = -b[2] / b[3])

ggplot(test, aes(x = glucose, y = mass)) +
  geom_point(aes(shape = diabetes), size = 2, colour = "grey30") +
  geom_abline(data = lines_t, aes(intercept = intercept, slope = slope, colour = t),
              linewidth = 1) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(neg = 1, pos = 17)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("0.3" = "blue", "0.5" = "red", "0.7" = "purple")) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(40, 200), ylim = c(18, 68)) +
  labs(x = "Glucose (mg/dL)", y = "BMI (kg/m²)", shape = "Measured", colour = "Threshold",
       title = "Three thresholds, three parallel boundaries")
```

Everyone to the right of a line is predicted `pos` at that threshold. Count
them:

```{r}
test_probs <- predict(log_fit, new_data = test, type = "prob")$.pred_pos

c(t_0.3 = sum(test_probs >= 0.3), t_0.5 = sum(test_probs >= 0.5),
  t_0.7 = sum(test_probs >= 0.7))
```

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Think about it
Lowering the threshold from 0.5 to 0.3 more than doubles the number of test
patients called `pos`. In the language of Exercise 4.3, what happens to the
sensitivity and the specificity, and where do you see that on the plot?
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
74 patients are called `pos` at 0.3, 35 at 0.5 and 19 at 0.7. Moving the line
to the left (0.3) brings more of the triangles onto the `pos` side, so the
sensitivity rises, but it also brings over many circles, so the specificity
falls. Moving it right (0.7) does the opposite. The model, its coefficients
and the tilt of the line are the same; only the decision changed.
:::
:::

### Part 3 — When a straight line cannot work

`data/sodium_delirium.csv` holds 500 older patients admitted to hospital: their
age, their blood sodium in mmol/L (normal is about 135 to 145), and whether
they developed delirium during the admission. If you do not have it yet,
[**download `sodium_delirium.csv`**](data/sodium_delirium.csv){download="sodium_delirium.csv"}
into your `data` folder.

```{r}
delirium <- read_csv("data/sodium_delirium.csv") |>
  mutate(delirium = factor(delirium, levels = c("no", "yes")))

test_rows_d <- seq(1, nrow(delirium), by = 5)     # every fifth patient is held back
train_d <- delirium[-test_rows_d, ]
test_d  <- delirium[test_rows_d, ]

count(train_d, delirium)
```

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
ggplot(train_d, aes(x = sodium, y = age, shape = delirium, colour = delirium)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(no = 1, yes = 17)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(no = "steelblue", yes = "darkorange")) +
  labs(x = "Sodium (mmol/L)", y = "Age (years)", shape = "Delirium", colour = "Delirium",
       title = "Training patients")
```

Delirium is common when sodium is **too low and when it is too high**, and
rarer in between. Fit the same kind of model as before, with age and sodium:

```{r}
line_fit <- log_model |>
  fit(delirium ~ age + sodium, data = train_d)

line_fit$fit$coefficients
```

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
grid_d <- expand_grid(sodium = seq(114, 163, by = 0.5), age = seq(60, 98, by = 0.5)) |>
  mutate(sodium_dev2 = (sodium - 140)^2)

delirium_map <- function(fit, title) {
  grid_d$prob <- predict(fit, new_data = grid_d, type = "prob")$.pred_yes
  ggplot(grid_d, aes(x = sodium, y = age)) +
    geom_raster(aes(fill = prob)) +
    geom_contour(aes(z = prob), breaks = 0.5, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.8) +
    geom_point(data = test_d, aes(shape = delirium), size = 1.5) +
    scale_fill_gradient2(low = "steelblue", mid = "white", high = "darkorange",
                         midpoint = 0.5, limits = c(0, 1)) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = c(no = 1, yes = 17)) +
    labs(x = "Sodium (mmol/L)", y = "Age (years)",
         fill = "Probability\nof delirium", shape = "Test patients", title = title)
}

delirium_map(line_fit, "Logistic regression: age + sodium")
```

The weight for sodium is almost exactly 0, and the map has no boundary at all:
the probability never reaches 0.5, so the model says `no` for every patient.
A straight line has to put "high risk" on one side. Here the high-risk patients
are on **both** sides, so the best straight line the model can find is one that
hardly uses sodium.

#### Task 3a — Give the model a predictor it can use

How far sodium is from normal matters, not which direction. Make a new column,
the squared distance from 140, and add it to the model. The model is still a
logistic regression, linear in the predictors you give it, but one of those
predictors is now curved in sodium.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
train_d <- train_d |> mutate(sodium_dev2 = (sodium - 140)^2)
test_d  <- test_d  |> mutate(sodium_dev2 = (sodium - 140)^2)

curve_fit <- log_model |>
  fit(delirium ~ age + sodium + ______, data = train_d)

curve_fit$fit$coefficients
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
Add the name of the new column to the formula, after a `+`.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
train_d <- train_d |> mutate(sodium_dev2 = (sodium - 140)^2)
test_d  <- test_d  |> mutate(sodium_dev2 = (sodium - 140)^2)

curve_fit <- log_model |>
  fit(delirium ~ age + sodium + sodium_dev2, data = train_d)

curve_fit$fit$coefficients
```

The weight for `sodium_dev2` is positive (0.023): the further sodium is from
140, in either direction, the higher the log-odds of delirium. Age now has a
clear positive weight too (0.039).
:::
:::

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
delirium_map(curve_fit, "Logistic regression: age + sodium + (sodium - 140)²")
```

A tree needs no new column: it can split on sodium twice.

```{r}
tree_fit <- decision_tree() |>
  set_engine("rpart") |>
  set_mode("classification") |>
  fit(delirium ~ age + sodium, data = train_d)

tree_fit
```

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
delirium_map(tree_fit, "Decision tree: age + sodium")
```

How often is each model right on the 100 test patients, and what does each say
about an 80-year-old with a low, a normal and a high sodium?

```{r}
data.frame(
  model = c("straight line", "with (sodium - 140)²", "tree", "always says no"),
  accuracy = c(mean(predict(line_fit,  new_data = test_d)$.pred_class == test_d$delirium),
               mean(predict(curve_fit, new_data = test_d)$.pred_class == test_d$delirium),
               mean(predict(tree_fit,  new_data = test_d)$.pred_class == test_d$delirium),
               mean(test_d$delirium == "no")))

patients <- data.frame(age = 80, sodium = c(126, 140, 154)) |>
  mutate(sodium_dev2 = (sodium - 140)^2)

patients |>
  mutate(straight_line = predict(line_fit,  new_data = patients, type = "prob")$.pred_yes,
         with_squared  = predict(curve_fit, new_data = patients, type = "prob")$.pred_yes,
         tree          = predict(tree_fit,  new_data = patients, type = "prob")$.pred_yes)
```

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Think about it
1. The straight-line model is right for 72% of the test patients. Is that a
   good model?
2. The straight-line model says sodium hardly matters. Is that true?
3. Describe the boundary of the model with the squared term, and of the tree.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
1. No. Always saying `no` is also right for 72%: the model says `no` to
   everyone and has learned nothing useful. Compare every accuracy with that
   baseline.
2. No. Sodium matters a great deal, but in both directions, which a straight
   line cannot express. An 80-year-old gets 0.33, 0.32 and 0.31 from the
   straight line whatever their sodium; the model with the squared term gives
   0.88, 0.08 and 0.91. A weight near 0 means "no straight-line relationship",
   not "no relationship".
3. The squared term gives two curved lines: delirium is predicted when sodium
   is below about 130 or above about 150, and the normal band narrows slightly
   with age (about 128 to 151 at 65, about 131 to 149 at 95). The tree gives
   three vertical bands: sodium below 130.5, 130.5 to 149.5, and 149.5 or
   above; it does not use age at all. Both are right for 88% of the test
   patients.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Learning points
- The decision boundary is where the predicted probability equals the
  threshold. For a logistic regression that is where the log-odds equal
  $\log\big(t/(1-t)\big)$: 0 for a threshold of 0.5.
- A logistic regression's boundary is straight (flat) in its predictors.
  Changing the threshold moves it without changing its tilt.
- When the risk is high at both ends of a measurement, no straight line can
  separate the classes, and a weight near 0 can hide a strong relationship.
- A boundary can bend if you give the model a curved predictor, such as a
  squared term, or use a model that bends on its own, such as a tree.
:::

### Packages and data

```{python}
# Packages for this exercise. If one is missing, install it once from a terminal
# (in a Jupyter notebook, type %pip instead of pip):
# pip install pandas numpy matplotlib scikit-learn

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, export_text
```

The same 750 people and the same split as in Exercise 4.1.

```{python}
diabetes = pd.read_csv("data/diabetes_clean.csv")
diabetes = diabetes[["glucose", "mass", "diabetes"]]

is_test = diabetes.index % 5 == 0               # every fifth person is held back
train = diabetes[~is_test]
test  = diabetes[is_test]
```

### Part 1 — Where the class changes

Fit the model from Exercise 4.1, Part 2: diabetes from glucose and BMI.

```{python}
log_model = LogisticRegression(C=np.inf)
log_model.fit(train[["glucose", "mass"]], train["diabetes"])

b0 = log_model.intercept_[0]
b1, b2 = log_model.coef_[0]          # glucose, BMI
print("intercept:", b0)
print("weights (glucose, BMI):", b1, b2)
```

The model is a straight line on the log-odds scale (Exercise 4.2):

$$\text{log-odds} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{glucose} + \beta_2 \times \text{BMI}$$

With a threshold of 0.5, the class changes where the probability is 0.5. A
probability of 0.5 is odds of 1 and **log-odds of 0**. So the boundary is every
combination of glucose and BMI where

$$\beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{glucose} + \beta_2 \times \text{BMI} = 0$$

For a given BMI, solve for glucose:

$$\text{glucose} = \frac{-\beta_0 - \beta_2 \times \text{BMI}}{\beta_1}$$

#### Task 1a — The boundary at a BMI of 30 and of 45

Round the coefficients printed above to four significant figures and calculate,
by hand, the glucose at which the class changes for a BMI of 30. Then do the
same for a BMI of 45.

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
boundary_30 = (-(______) - ______ * 30) / ______
boundary_45 = (-(______) - ______ * 45) / ______
print(boundary_30, boundary_45)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
In order: the intercept, the BMI weight, and the glucose weight. The intercept
is negative, so minus the intercept is a positive number.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
boundary_30 = (-(-7.004) - 0.06437 * 30) / 0.03355
boundary_45 = (-(-7.004) - 0.06437 * 45) / 0.03355
print(boundary_30, boundary_45)
```

At a BMI of 30 the class changes at a glucose of about 151 mg/dL; at a BMI of
45, at about 122.
:::
:::

Check it with `.predict_proba()`: a patient on the boundary should get a
probability of 0.5.

```{python}
log_model.predict_proba(pd.DataFrame({"glucose": [151.2], "mass": [30]}))
```

Every point on the boundary satisfies one linear equation in glucose and BMI,
so the boundary is a **straight line**. Here it is, drawn from the
coefficients, over the test patients:

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
glucose_line = np.array([40, 200])
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for cls, mk, colour in [("neg", "o", "steelblue"), ("pos", "^", "darkorange")]:
    rows = test[test["diabetes"] == cls]
    ax.scatter(rows["glucose"], rows["mass"], marker=mk, color=colour, s=20, label=cls)
# the boundary written as BMI = (-b0 - b1 * glucose) / b2
ax.plot(glucose_line, (-b0 - b1 * glucose_line) / b2, color="black", linewidth=2)
ax.scatter([151.2, 122.4], [30, 45], color="red", s=50, zorder=3)
ax.set_xlim(40, 200)
ax.set_ylim(18, 68)
ax.set_xlabel("Glucose (mg/dL)")
ax.set_ylabel("BMI (kg/m²)")
ax.legend(title="Measured")
ax.set_title("The decision boundary at a threshold of 0.5")
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Think about it
1. The model is right for 76% of the test patients. Looking at the plot, why
   can no straight line do much better with these two measurements?
2. A model with three predictors (glucose, BMI and age) also has a boundary.
   What shape would it be?
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
1. Patients with and without diabetes overlap heavily: there are triangles
   well to the left of the line and circles well to the right. Glucose and BMI
   do not hold enough information to separate them, whatever line you draw.
2. Still flat: one linear equation in three measurements is a flat plane in
   three dimensions. A logistic regression always has a flat boundary in the
   predictors you give it.
:::
:::

### Part 2 — The threshold moves the line

Exercise 4.3 changed the threshold. A threshold $t$ is a probability, so it has
a log-odds, $\log\big(t / (1 - t)\big)$, and the boundary is where the model's
log-odds equal it:

$$\beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{glucose} + \beta_2 \times \text{BMI} = \log\left(\frac{t}{1-t}\right)$$

Only the right-hand side changes, so the line keeps its tilt and moves
sideways.

#### Task 2a — The log-odds of three thresholds

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
thresholds = pd.DataFrame({"t": [0.3, 0.5, 0.7]})
thresholds["log_odds"] = np.log(______ / (1 - ______))
thresholds["glucose_at_BMI_30"] = (thresholds["log_odds"] - b0 - b2 * 30) / b1

thresholds
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
Both blanks are the threshold column, `thresholds["t"]`.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
thresholds = pd.DataFrame({"t": [0.3, 0.5, 0.7]})
thresholds["log_odds"] = np.log(thresholds["t"] / (1 - thresholds["t"]))
thresholds["glucose_at_BMI_30"] = (thresholds["log_odds"] - b0 - b2 * 30) / b1

thresholds
```

The log-odds are −0.847, 0 and 0.847. At a BMI of 30 the class changes at a
glucose of 126, 151 and 176 mg/dL.
:::
:::

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for cls, mk in [("neg", "o"), ("pos", "^")]:
    rows = test[test["diabetes"] == cls]
    ax.scatter(rows["glucose"], rows["mass"], marker=mk, color="grey", s=20, label=cls)
for t, colour in [(0.3, "blue"), (0.5, "red"), (0.7, "purple")]:
    lo = np.log(t / (1 - t))
    ax.plot(glucose_line, (lo - b0 - b1 * glucose_line) / b2, color=colour,
            linewidth=2, label=f"threshold {t}")
ax.set_xlim(40, 200)
ax.set_ylim(18, 68)
ax.set_xlabel("Glucose (mg/dL)")
ax.set_ylabel("BMI (kg/m²)")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
ax.set_title("Three thresholds, three parallel boundaries")
plt.show()
```

Everyone to the right of a line is predicted `pos` at that threshold. Count
them:

```{python}
test_probs = log_model.predict_proba(test[["glucose", "mass"]])[:, 1]

print("t = 0.3:", (test_probs >= 0.3).sum())
print("t = 0.5:", (test_probs >= 0.5).sum())
print("t = 0.7:", (test_probs >= 0.7).sum())
```

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Think about it
Lowering the threshold from 0.5 to 0.3 more than doubles the number of test
patients called `pos`. In the language of Exercise 4.3, what happens to the
sensitivity and the specificity, and where do you see that on the plot?
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
74 patients are called `pos` at 0.3, 35 at 0.5 and 19 at 0.7. Moving the line
to the left (0.3) brings more of the triangles onto the `pos` side, so the
sensitivity rises, but it also brings over many circles, so the specificity
falls. Moving it right (0.7) does the opposite. The model, its coefficients
and the tilt of the line are the same; only the decision changed.
:::
:::

### Part 3 — When a straight line cannot work

`data/sodium_delirium.csv` holds 500 older patients admitted to hospital: their
age, their blood sodium in mmol/L (normal is about 135 to 145), and whether
they developed delirium during the admission. If you do not have it yet,
[**download `sodium_delirium.csv`**](data/sodium_delirium.csv){download="sodium_delirium.csv"}
into your `data` folder.

```{python}
delirium = pd.read_csv("data/sodium_delirium.csv")

is_test_d = delirium.index % 5 == 0             # every fifth patient is held back
train_d = delirium[~is_test_d].copy()
test_d  = delirium[is_test_d].copy()

train_d["delirium"].value_counts()
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for cls, mk, colour in [("no", "o", "steelblue"), ("yes", "^", "darkorange")]:
    rows = train_d[train_d["delirium"] == cls]
    ax.scatter(rows["sodium"], rows["age"], marker=mk, color=colour, s=20, label=cls)
ax.set_xlabel("Sodium (mmol/L)")
ax.set_ylabel("Age (years)")
ax.legend(title="Delirium")
ax.set_title("Training patients")
plt.show()
```

Delirium is common when sodium is **too low and when it is too high**, and
rarer in between. Fit the same kind of model as before, with age and sodium:

```{python}
line_model = LogisticRegression(C=np.inf)
line_model.fit(train_d[["age", "sodium"]], train_d["delirium"])

print("intercept:", line_model.intercept_)
print("weights (age, sodium):", line_model.coef_)
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
from matplotlib.colors import LinearSegmentedColormap

S, A = np.meshgrid(np.arange(114, 163.5, 0.5), np.arange(60, 98.5, 0.5))
grid_d = pd.DataFrame({"age": A.ravel(), "sodium": S.ravel()})
grid_d["sodium_dev2"] = (grid_d["sodium"] - 140) ** 2
blue_orange = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("bo", ["steelblue", "white", "darkorange"])

def delirium_map(model, columns, title):
    prob = model.predict_proba(grid_d[columns])[:, 1].reshape(S.shape)
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    im = ax.pcolormesh(S, A, prob, cmap=blue_orange, vmin=0, vmax=1, shading="auto")
    if prob.min() < 0.5 < prob.max():
        ax.contour(S, A, prob, levels=[0.5], colors="black")
    no, yes = test_d[test_d["delirium"] == "no"], test_d[test_d["delirium"] == "yes"]
    ax.scatter(no["sodium"], no["age"], marker="o", facecolors="none",
               edgecolors="black", s=20, label="test: no")
    ax.scatter(yes["sodium"], yes["age"], marker="^", color="black", s=20,
               label="test: yes")
    fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, label="Probability of delirium")
    ax.set_xlabel("Sodium (mmol/L)")
    ax.set_ylabel("Age (years)")
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=8)
    plt.show()

delirium_map(line_model, ["age", "sodium"], "Logistic regression: age + sodium")
```

The weight for sodium is almost exactly 0, and the map has no boundary at all:
the probability never reaches 0.5, so the model says `no` for every patient.
A straight line has to put "high risk" on one side. Here the high-risk patients
are on **both** sides, so the best straight line the model can find is one that
hardly uses sodium.

#### Task 3a — Give the model a predictor it can use

How far sodium is from normal matters, not which direction. Make a new column,
the squared distance from 140, and add it to the model. The model is still a
logistic regression, linear in the predictors you give it, but one of those
predictors is now curved in sodium.

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
train_d["sodium_dev2"] = (train_d["sodium"] - 140) ** 2
test_d["sodium_dev2"]  = (test_d["sodium"] - 140) ** 2

curve_columns = ["age", "sodium", "______"]
curve_model = LogisticRegression(C=np.inf)
curve_model.fit(train_d[curve_columns], train_d["delirium"])

print("weights (age, sodium, sodium_dev2):", curve_model.coef_)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
The third column is the name of the new column you just made.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
train_d["sodium_dev2"] = (train_d["sodium"] - 140) ** 2
test_d["sodium_dev2"]  = (test_d["sodium"] - 140) ** 2

curve_columns = ["age", "sodium", "sodium_dev2"]
curve_model = LogisticRegression(C=np.inf)
curve_model.fit(train_d[curve_columns], train_d["delirium"])

print("weights (age, sodium, sodium_dev2):", curve_model.coef_)
```

The weight for `sodium_dev2` is positive (0.023): the further sodium is from
140, in either direction, the higher the log-odds of delirium. Age now has a
clear positive weight too (0.039).
:::
:::

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
delirium_map(curve_model, curve_columns,
             "Logistic regression: age + sodium + (sodium - 140)²")
```

A tree needs no new column: it can split on sodium twice.

```{python}
tree_model = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=2, random_state=0)
tree_model.fit(train_d[["age", "sodium"]], train_d["delirium"])

print(export_text(tree_model, feature_names=["age", "sodium"]))
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
delirium_map(tree_model, ["age", "sodium"], "Decision tree: age + sodium")
```

How often is each model right on the 100 test patients, and what does each say
about an 80-year-old with a low, a normal and a high sodium?

```{python}
print(pd.DataFrame({
    "model": ["straight line", "with (sodium - 140)²", "tree", "always says no"],
    "accuracy": [line_model.score(test_d[["age", "sodium"]], test_d["delirium"]),
                 curve_model.score(test_d[curve_columns], test_d["delirium"]),
                 tree_model.score(test_d[["age", "sodium"]], test_d["delirium"]),
                 (test_d["delirium"] == "no").mean()]}))

patients = pd.DataFrame({"age": [80, 80, 80], "sodium": [126, 140, 154]})
patients["sodium_dev2"] = (patients["sodium"] - 140) ** 2
patients["straight_line"] = line_model.predict_proba(patients[["age", "sodium"]])[:, 1]
patients["with_squared"] = curve_model.predict_proba(patients[curve_columns])[:, 1]
patients["tree"] = tree_model.predict_proba(patients[["age", "sodium"]])[:, 1]
patients
```

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Think about it
1. The straight-line model is right for 72% of the test patients. Is that a
   good model?
2. The straight-line model says sodium hardly matters. Is that true?
3. Describe the boundary of the model with the squared term, and of the tree.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
1. No. Always saying `no` is also right for 72%: the model says `no` to
   everyone and has learned nothing useful. Compare every accuracy with that
   baseline.
2. No. Sodium matters a great deal, but in both directions, which a straight
   line cannot express. An 80-year-old gets 0.33, 0.32 and 0.31 from the
   straight line whatever their sodium; the model with the squared term gives
   0.88, 0.08 and 0.91. A weight near 0 means "no straight-line relationship",
   not "no relationship".
3. The squared term gives two curved lines: delirium is predicted when sodium
   is below about 130 or above about 150, and the normal band narrows slightly
   with age (about 128 to 151 at 65, about 131 to 149 at 95). The tree gives
   three vertical bands of `yes`, `no`, `yes`, at sodium 130.5 and 149.5; it
   does not use age at all. (It also splits the low-sodium band at 127.5, but
   both halves still say `yes`.) Both are right for 88% of the test patients.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Learning points
- The decision boundary is where the predicted probability equals the
  threshold. For a logistic regression that is where the log-odds equal
  $\log\big(t/(1-t)\big)$: 0 for a threshold of 0.5.
- A logistic regression's boundary is straight (flat) in its predictors.
  Changing the threshold moves it without changing its tilt.
- When the risk is high at both ends of a measurement, no straight line can
  separate the classes, and a weight near 0 can hide a strong relationship.
- A boundary can bend if you give the model a curved predictor, such as a
  squared term, or use a model that bends on its own, such as a tree.
:::

::::::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::: {.instructor}
**Teaching choice.** Part 1 links the map students saw in Exercise 4.1 to the
coefficients of Exercise 4.2; Part 2 links it to the thresholds of Exercise
4.3. Part 3 uses a simulated dataset (`scripts/make_data.R`,
`data/PROVENANCE.txt`) built so that the risk is U-shaped in sodium.

**Expected values.** Glucose and BMI model: −7.004, 0.03355, 0.06437;
boundary BMI = 108.8 − 0.521 × glucose; at BMI 30 glucose 151.2, at BMI 45
122.4. Thresholds 0.3, 0.5, 0.7: log-odds −0.847, 0, 0.847; glucose at BMI 30
125.9, 151.2, 176.4; test patients called `pos` 74, 35, 19. Sodium data: 500
patients, 148 with delirium; training 400 (120 yes), test 100 (28 yes).
Straight line: −2.112, age 0.0228, sodium −0.0034; predicted probabilities
0.22 to 0.42, so `no` for everyone; accuracy 0.72 = baseline. With
`sodium_dev2`: −6.913, 0.0389, 0.0098, 0.0232; accuracy 0.88; boundary at age
80 sodium 129.6 and 150.0. Tree: R default 3 leaves (sodium < 130.5 → 0.82,
130.5–149.5 → 0.10, ≥ 149.5 → 0.80); Python `max_depth=2` 4 leaves (extra
split at 127.5, both `yes`); both 0.88. Patient aged 80, sodium 126 / 140 /
154: line 0.33 / 0.32 / 0.31, squared 0.88 / 0.08 / 0.91, tree 0.82 (Python
0.90, its extra leaf) / 0.10 / 0.80.

**Common failures.** (1) Forgetting that the boundary uses log-odds 0, not
probability 0, and solving β0 + β1 glucose + β2 BMI = 0.5. (2) Dropping the
minus sign of the intercept in Task 1a. (3) In Task 3a, adding the column to
`train_d` but not to `test_d`, so prediction fails with a missing column.

**Timing.** Part 1 fifteen minutes, Part 2 ten, Part 3 twenty.
:::
